Gauche

GOHSH · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Gauche is unsophisticated and awkward; socially clumsy.

Correcting the professor's grammar in front of the entire lecture hall was, several students agreed, more than a little gauche.

Worked Example

Bringing up the bride's ex-boyfriend during the wedding toast struck every single guest as spectacularly gauche.

Behavior that's clumsy, tactless, and clearly out of step with the social moment is exactly what gauche describes.

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

tactless

tactless: lacking sensitivity in dealing with others

clumsy: lacking social or physical grace

Antonyms

tactful

tactful: careful not to offend or upset others

polished

polished: refined and socially graceful

How Strong Is It? — awkward → gauche → tactless

awkward vs. gauche

awkward vs. gauche: His awkward joke landed with a few uncomfortable laughs before the room moved on.

tactless vs. gauche

tactless vs. gauche: Tactless is harsher than gauche: a gauche remark is merely clumsy and unpolished, while a tactless one -- asking a grieving widow about the will at the funeral -- actually wounds.

Build the Word

The pieces

origin — gauche

origin — gauche: left (French)

Put it together

Put it together: Gauche is French for 'left' (as opposed to the right side). For centuries, many cultures unfairly associated the left hand with clumsiness, so gauche came to describe someone socially awkward -- the same unfair pattern that gave Latin sinister ('left') its meaning of 'evil' or 'unlucky.'

A word borrowed the same way: sinister

A word borrowed the same way: sinister: English sinister tells the same story in a different language: in Latin it meant simply 'left,' and the same unfair left-equals-bad thinking pushed it toward 'evil' and 'unlucky.' Gauche and sinister share that pattern, not a root -- one is French, the other Latin.
